title: New MOHRE Labour Classification System 2026
description: There is a recent company classification in the UAE, as well as a MOHRE labour card fees. Learn more here with us!

If you are establishing a company in the region and want to obtain your MOHRE labour card, you should be familiar with the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization. This ministry oversees labor laws and safeguards businesses and workers nationwide. In doing so, it achieves equilibrium and allows positive interactions among the participants, strengthening the economy and more.

In this article, we will be talking about the MOHRE and the most recent UAE labour category list. Let us observe:

Do you know what MOHRE is?

The MOHRE, or Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization, is the authority that governs everything pertaining to work. Additionally, it steps in when contractors or workers do not follow the rules established in their limited or unlimited contracts. The MOL also suggests and enacts labor rules and regulations in the UAE.

In resolving disputes between employees and employers, it serves as the court of first instance in a similar manner. Through dialogue and compromise, it advances a practical resolution for the participants in this instance. One of the crucial things that all international workers who reside in the nation should be aware of is this.

The June 30, 2026 deadline you cannot miss

This is the most urgent update for any company employing Emirati nationals, and it sits on top of the classification system rather than replacing it.

Effective January 1, 2026, MOHRE raised the minimum monthly wage for Emiratis in the private sector to AED 6,000, up from the previous AED 5,000 floor, as part of a phased Emiratisation wage strategy that has moved from AED 4,000 to 5,000 to 6,000 over recent years. The new floor applies automatically to any new, renewed, or amended citizen work permit issued from that date.

For Emiratis already on payroll before January 1, 2026, MOHRE granted a grace period: employers have until June 30, 2026 to amend contracts and bring salaries up to the AED 6,000 minimum. That’s roughly two weeks away from today.

From July 1, 2026, companies that haven’t adjusted will face two specific consequences:

Any Emirati employee still earning below AED 6,000 will stop counting toward that company’s Emiratisation quota, which can knock a company down a classification tier on its own.

MOHRE will suspend the issuance of new work permits for the establishment entirely until salaries are brought into line.

This deadline is being enforced automatically: MOHRE has stated it is sending notifications through its smart app and service channels, so companies are expected to already be aware. If you employ even one Emirati national on a salary below AED 6,000, this should be the first thing you check, ahead of everything else in this guide.

2. Learn about the MOHRE labour card

The MOHRE labour card is an essential document for workers in the. The UAE labor card acts as a form of identity and has to be held at all times. It is issued by recognized institutions such as the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization (MOHRE) or the applicable free zone.

The labour card is an essential identity document that serves as a fundamental point of reference for both the worker and their employer, ensuring the smooth operation of the labor market. There is a lot to know about it, such as:

  • The worker’s name.
  • Occupation.
  • Employer.
  • Nationality.
  • Expiration date.
  • Personal identification number.
  • Work permit number.
  • MOHRE labour card number.

The UAE officials no longer print physical labor cards; therefore, be aware of this and make a duplicate of your labor card after downloading it.

Regardless of their nationality or the nature of their employment, all employees in the United Arab Emirates must have a UAE labor card. This refers to all employees in the nation, domestic and foreign, working in both the public and private sectors.

Workers as well as employers must fulfill the requirements below in order to qualify for a UAE labor card.

For employees:

  • The minimum age requirement is 18, and the maximum age limit is 60.
  • They must have the academic credentials necessary for the position.
  • They need to pass a medical test and get a certificate from their place of origin.

For employers:

  • Employers must maintain accurate records and discard any outdated labor cards.
  • The employee’s pay must be commensurate with their field.
  • Employers are responsible for ensuring that their organizations follow the rules established by the Ministry.

3. Know the new labour card category in UAE

A new classification system for enterprises in the UAE has been revealed by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization (MOHRE), which will now be divided into three levels. Since June 1, 2022, this new company category UAE classification system has been in place.

This rating is according to how much companies abide by the new UAE labor regulations, including the protection of workers’ rights, the pay protection system, and the promotion of cultural and social diversity.

In addition, the system will impose new work permit fees depending on the worker’s level of expertise, whether they are employed domestically or abroad, and the type of business. Companies must thoroughly comprehend the changes because the fees list has undergone major changes.

Here is the new system of classification:

Tier 1

Companies that fully commit to the UAE’s policy supporting diversity as well as the labor law, wage protection system, labor market regulation resolutions, and workers’ rights protection fall under this category.

To qualify for Tier 1, businesses must additionally meet at least one of these requirements:

  • Increase the Emiratization rate by at least three times compared to the goal.
  • Collaborate with the “Nafis” initiative to train no less than 500 citizens yearly.
  • Identified as an education and job placement facility that promotes the Workforce Planning Policy’s implementation by fostering cultural diversity in the United Arab Emirates.
  • Being engaged in the targeted activities and sectors that the Council of Ministers has decided based on the ministry’s choice.
  • Being a young citizen-owned business that adheres to accepted standards.

Tier 2

Similar to tier 1, the level of a company’s commitment to the labor legislation, wage protection system, labor market regulations, workers’ rights protection, and UAE diversity policy determines where it falls within this category.

This tier is further split into more specific classification tiers A, B, C, or D. When awarding work permits, this will be determined based on the ratio of competent employees and the degree of that company’s commitment to intercultural diversity.

The company will be in tier 3 if it does not meet this requirement.

  • Category 2A: If a company employs 40% or more skilled people overall and at least 50% of its workforce is of other nationalities (multicultural), it will fall into Category 2A.
  • Set 2B: If a company employs between 10% and 40% skilled people overall and has a minimum of 50% national diversity (multicultural), it will be Category 2B.
  • Category 2C: A company will be categorized as Category 2C if it employs between 5% and 10% skilled workers overall and at least 50% of its employees are of other nationalities (multicultural).
  • Category 2D: A company will be categorized as Category 2D if it employs less than 5% skilled people overall or has a nationality (multicultural) ratio of less than 50%.

Tier 3

Tier 3 companies are those that

  • Are breaching the UAE Labour Law, executive orders, labor market regulations, and requirements for safeguarding labor rights.
  • Have a lack of dedication to promoting demographic and cultural diversity in the UAE labor market.
  • Other offenses outlined in Ministerial Resolution No. 209 of 2022, including hiring or recruiting workers without proper documentation; giving the Ministry inaccurate data, documents, or information; failing to adhere to regulations governing workers’ wages, housing, and safety; engaging in false Emiratization practices; or committing other serious offenses.

Companies in this class will probably face fines and other sanctions for their infractions. After serving the necessary time in this category, correcting the violations, and paying the relevant fines, a corporation may, nonetheless, ascend from this tier into tier 2 or tier 3.

See the labour card fees

According to the scheme, new MOHRE labor card payments will depend primarily on the worker’s skill level, whether they work domestically or abroad, and the type of business. Companies must thoroughly comprehend the changes because the fees list has undergone major changes.

The fee for granting a work permit to an outsider is Dh 200 for each of the three tiers. Also, the fee for authorizing a work permit for the first category of companies is Dh 300 for two years, regardless of the worker’s skill level.

The second-tier companies must pay the following fees to MOHRE services:

  • 2A category: DH 1,200 and DH 500, respectively, for semi-skilled workers.
  • 2B category: For skilled workers, the rate is DH 1,000, while for semi-skilled workers, it is DH 2,200.
  • 2C category: DH 1,500 and DH 2,700, respectively, for skilled and semi-skilled labor.
  • 2D category: 2000 DH for expert laborers and 3,200 DH for semi-skilled laborers.

Regardless of the worker’s skill level, a work permit costs Dh 5,000 for foreign nationals for businesses in the tier 3 company category in the UAE.

How applications actually get processed now: the Work Bundle platform

One of the more significant operational changes since the 2022 classification rules is how applications actually move through MOHRE. The ministry has consolidated what used to be five separate systems into a single platform, known as Work Bundle, that has cut the documents required from 16 to 5, the process steps from 15 to 5, in-person visits from 7 to 2, and total processing time from roughly 30 working days down to about 5.

In practice, this means most classification-related paperwork, permit applications, and renewals can now be completed almost entirely online, with company tier and worker skill level pulled automatically into the fee calculation at submission. It also means errors in self-managed applications surface, and get penalised, faster than they used to.

How to move up a tier

Since classification now directly intersects with the 2026 wage rules, moving up a tier is both a cost-saving move and, increasingly, a way to avoid being blocked from issuing new permits. The most effective levers are:

Increasing the proportion of skilled workers on payroll, which helps move a company from 2D toward 2A. Hiring and properly registering UAE nationals through Nafis and meeting or exceeding Emiratisation targets. Bringing every Emirati salary up to the AED 6,000 minimum before June 30, 2026, since failing to do so removes those employees from your Emiratisation count entirely. Maintaining full Wages Protection System compliance and addressing any outstanding violations before they compound into a Tier 3 classification. Keeping workforce nationality diversity above the 50% (Tier 2) or below the 20% single-nationality concentration (mainland) thresholds.

FAQs:

What is the new MOHRE Labour Classification System in the UAE?

It’s a framework ranking companies based on Emiratisation efforts, diversity, and compliance with labour laws.

Why did MOHRE introduce the new classification system?

The goal is to promote fair employment practices and encourage Emiratisation by rewarding compliant companies with benefits.

How are companies classified under the new MOHRE system?

Companies are grouped into categories (1, 2, or 3) depending on their adherence to labour rules and hiring diversity.

How does the classification affect a company’s operations in the UAE?

Better classifications mean lower fees for work permits and faster processing of government services.

How can a company improve its MOHRE classification?

Companies can improve it by hiring Emiratis, ensuring timely salaries, maintaining compliance, and making their workplace more inclusive.
